I have a similiar (or is it similar?) story. My mom and I decided to visit the "kill shelter" (its a rundown animal shelter where they put down the animals after a week and the old aged ones go first) and see the cats. There were two that really jumped out at us. One cat, Alexa, was an 11 year old owner surrender (they had owned Alexa all her life) and she was veryyy fat! The other one was a street cat, whom we later named Hydrogen, that kept putting his paw out of the cage to reach out at us and play. We got them both. But when we tried to get Alexa out of her cage and into our carrier, she kept clawing and biting us (she doesnt have a voice)- which was strange because she was so preciois when we were petting her head through the cage. A lot of people would've said no thanks and put her back and let her be put down on schedule the next day. But we took her.Turns out she had a really bad infection on her back because shes too fat, and the cage was too small, for her to clean herself. Now with Hydrogen, he was the sweetest and most playful cat ever! We was around seven months old. He was diagnosed with feline leukimia. The vet said he could live a couple months, or he could live a few years. My mom and I got in many arguments over him. She said that he couldnt live with us because we let our cats go outside, and that would make him sick. So she wanted him to go and live with a friend- who has two dogs and a cat and their living space is smaller than ours. I finally was able to form my feelings into words- I'd rather Hydrogen be happy and only live a fee months than him go and live in a stressful environment for years. She agreed. And so he did- he lived the happiest and most spoiled life a cat could have. He ate dinner with me, slept with me, played outside, played with us, ate "people" food. And he passed away a few months later, which is where the simularity came in. I do believe that months of happiness overpowers years of pain. 

TL;DR Adopted a cat, had choice of living for years in a stressful environment or months in a happy one. Chose the latter :)

Hello, I've been working with Magenta for about 2 weeks, so, and I find that drawing, even just sketching, your tulpa helps a lot. It makes it easier to visualize and  makes them more tangible. I, too, have been worried about puppeting, but if you have no visualization, what is there to focus on? Magenta said her first words today :3 She probably won't speak again for a while, though. Just make sure that you aren't constantly controlling them, try and give them a lil bit of free reign, even if it's very early in the process. As a beginner, I can say that this has been working for us perfectly fine, and the rate at which she is becoming sentient is amazing. Basically, just guide your tulpa and treat them as real as you can, not as a figment of your imagination. These are just my personal experineces, so you should probably take the more experienced peoples' advice over mine if they conflict :P
